name: Fathom
tagline: Lightweight website analytics that runs without cookies.
description: Fathom is lightweight website analytics: one script tag, one dashboard, and no cookie banner between the site and its traffic.
pros: Installation is one script tag, so putting Fathom on a site does not need a release cycle for each metric.
Collection is cookie-free, so the consent-banner step most analytics tools require does not apply to a Fathom install.
The dashboard is one screen of figures that a new reader can interpret without being taught a report builder.
Pricing is recorded as a fixed monthly band of $14-54/mo on a pageview unit, tying cost to traffic rather than to seats.
Two blog entries in this repository list Fathom beside Plausible, which keeps the cookieless shortlist down to two names.
cons: One dashboard is also one level of depth: funnel, retention, and cohort questions have nowhere in Fathom to be answered.
Because the billing unit is pageviews, a traffic spike raises the bill even though the site itself has not changed.
Scope stops at the website, so in-app events, account-level reporting, and journeys across an application are outside what is collected.

content.title: One script, one dashboard
content.body: Fathom is a website analytics service built to be installed once and then left alone. A single script tag is the whole integration surface: there is no event taxonomy to design, no tag manager to maintain, and no per-metric code to ship. What comes back is one dashboard of traffic figures, kept deliberately flat so that reading it does not require training. Nothing in this write-up comes from installing Fathom; it is assembled from vendor documentation and the repository entries that mention the product, so the setup claims above should be read as documentation rather than field notes.

content.title: Cookieless collection and the consent question
content.body: Fathom records visits without placing cookies on the visitor's device, and that is the property which removes the usual consent-banner conversation. Two entries in this repository make the point independently: one cost blog describes Fathom as cookie-free tracking with simple dashboards and pageview-based pricing, and an alternatives blog describes it as privacy-focused analytics taking the same approach. The distinction matters legally as well as technically, because a site that writes no identifiers has a different consent posture from one that does. Exact obligations still depend on jurisdiction, which no dataset here can settle.

content.title: Reading the single dashboard
content.body: The reporting surface is a single page, and the items below are what it is built to show. Everything is arranged for a site owner who wants an answer in a glance rather than for an analyst assembling a model, so there is nothing to configure before the figures are legible. The same constraint sets the ceiling: when a number needs explaining there is no drill-down to reach for, because the dashboard reports rather than diagnoses.
items: Visit counts for the current period against the one before it
The pages that received the traffic
Referrers and campaign sources behind each visit
Device and browser breakdown of visitors
Automated bot traffic kept out of the totals

content.title: Pageview-based pricing
content.body: Our file lists Fathom under paid pricing at $14-54/mo, and this repository's analytics cost blog independently describes its pricing as pageview-based. Read together, the bill tracks how much traffic a site receives rather than how many people hold an account, which is a simpler unit than seats but a less predictable one during a launch or a press spike. No tier breakdown appears anywhere in our records, so what sits at each end of that band is not established here.

content.title: Fathom next to Google Analytics
content.body: This repository holds a direct comparison record between Fathom and Google Analytics, plus an alternatives blog dedicated to Google Analytics in which Fathom is named. The structural difference those pages imply is scope: Fathom's dashboard answers what happened on the site, while a general-purpose analytics suite carries user-level and event-level machinery that Fathom does not attempt. The comparison rows mark both products present on most criteria, which is generated boilerplate rather than a measured result; the useful signal is that the pages address a buyer looking to leave a large analytics suite.

content.title: A namesake worth ruling out
content.body: One entry in this repository's remote-work research groups Fathom with Otter.ai and Fireflies under meeting-assistant consolidation. That is a different product trading under the same name, and the market-share figure recorded alongside it belongs to that market rather than to web analytics. This review covers only the website analytics service documented elsewhere in our records. Anyone shortlisting tools from repository search results should check the domain first, so that two mentions of a name are not assumed to be one product.

content.title: Where a lightweight analyzer stops
content.body: Fathom's limits follow from its design rather than from unfinished work. A tool that declines to model individual behavior cannot answer retention, funnel, or account-level questions, and no amount of dashboard polish changes that. The pageview billing unit also means traffic volume drives cost while the feature set stays fixed. Teams expecting their site metrics to grow into product analytics outgrow Fathom quickly, and the honest answer at that point is a different category of tool rather than a larger Fathom plan.

content.title: Fit, caveats, and the record we hold
content.body: Fathom suits a site that wants clean traffic numbers, a privacy posture that does not depend on a consent banner, and a subscription priced in tens of dollars rather than by seat. It is the wrong instrument for anyone who needs to follow a visitor across an application or compare cohorts. Our file scores it 4.5 from 640 entries, and four of its thirteen comparison records pair it with tools from entirely different categories, so the pairings matter less than the rating does. Our records hold no security certifications for Fathom, so any compliance question has to go to the vendor directly.

faqs.question: Does Fathom really work without a consent banner?
faqs.answer: This repository describes Fathom as cookie-free tracking, which is what removes the banner requirement. Whether your site still needs one depends on everything else it loads, and on the rules that apply to you, not on Fathom alone.

faqs.question: Is the Fathom in this repository the analytics product or the meeting tool?
faqs.answer: The review file, the blog entries, and the comparison records all describe the website analytics service. One remote-work research file mentions a same-named meeting assistant, and its market-share note does not apply to this product.

faqs.question: How does Fathom's price behave as traffic grows?
faqs.answer: Our file records $14-54/mo and this repository's cost blog records pageview-based billing, so the bill follows traffic volume. No tier breakdown exists in our records to show where the steps fall.

faqs.question: Can Fathom stand in for Google Analytics?
faqs.answer: This repository holds a Fathom-versus-Google Analytics comparison and an alternatives blog naming Fathom. It covers site traffic well and does not attempt the user-level and event-level analysis a general suite carries.

faqs.question: What compliance records does this dataset hold for Fathom?
faqs.answer: None. No certification or attestation appears anywhere in our records for Fathom, so a compliance review has to start with the vendor's current documentation rather than with this record.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Very short — one script and one screen, with almost nothing to learn before the figures are readable.
whoShouldUse: Site owners, publishers, and small teams that want traffic figures without a consent banner and without a report builder in front of them.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need funnel, retention, or account-level product analysis, or anyone who must follow a single visitor beyond the page view.
